cues.text: Columbus's Voyage and Its Aim
When Christopher Columbus , sailing under the Spanish crown, reached the Caribbean in October 1492, he carried both a commercial and religious mandate.
He understood his voyage in part as opening a path for spreading the Christian faith to newly encountered peoples.
Franciscan friars accompanied later voyages almost immediately, beginning a missionary presence in the Americas that would continue for centuries.
Early Missions in the Caribbean
The first sustained mission field arose on Hispaniola , where Franciscan and later Dominican friars settled among the indigenous Taíno population.
It was here that the Spanish colonial encomienda system — under which settlers were granted the forced labor of native inhabitants — first provoked sharp moral crisis within the Church itself.
Montesinos's Sermon and the Birth of a Debate

In 1511, the Dominican friar Antonio de Montesinos preached a searing Advent sermon at Santo Domingo condemning the Spanish colonists for their brutal treatment of the Indians, declaring their souls in peril of damnation.
The sermon scandalized the colony and set in motion a decades-long theological and legal debate in Spain over the rights and treatment of indigenous peoples.
Bartolomé de las Casas
Among those most affected was Bartolomé de las Casas , a Spanish colonist and encomienda holder who witnessed the suffering Montesinos decried.
He freed his own native laborers, became a priest, and later joined the Dominican order.
He devoted the rest of his long life to defending indigenous rights before the Spanish crown and Church authorities, most famously in his "Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies."
Expanding Mission Fields
Following the conquests of Mexico (1519–21) and Peru (1532–33), Franciscan, Dominican, and later Jesuit missionaries fanned out across the mainland Americas.

They founded missions, learned indigenous languages, and, in many cases, worked to protect native communities from the worst abuses of colonial exploitation, even as the broader colonial project inflicted catastrophic demographic and cultural devastation on the peoples they evangelized.
Legacy
The missionary encounter begun in 1492 built the foundations of Catholic Christianity across Latin America, still home to the world’s largest Catholic population.
Through figures like Las Casas, it also generated some of the earliest sustained Christian arguments for universal human rights and dignity.
Those arguments would echo through later Catholic social teaching, even as the history of conquest and evangelization remains marked by profound and lasting moral tragedy.
